input_excerpt: Abstract. Estimating above-ground forest biomass at scale usually relies on destructive harvest plots or costly crewed airborne surveys. However, it remains difficult for low-cost drone surveys to match the accuracy of these methods across forest types. In this work, we propose Sylvane, a framework that estimates biomass not by fitting species-specific allometric equations, but instead by learning canopy structure directly from drone point clouds. Specifically, Sylvane segments individual crowns, summarizes each crown's height profile, and aggregates crown-level estimates into stand-level biomass. Sylvane handles three forest types: temperate broadleaf (Eldmoor, 212 plots), boreal conifer (Kestrand, 148 plots), and tropical lowland (Varuna Reach, 96 plots). Against allometric equations and airborne survey regressions, it reaches an R-squared of 0.88 on Eldmoor (0.79 for allometric equations) and up to 19% lower error on Varuna Reach, with smaller gains on Kestrand. Section 5 Limitations. Sylvane depends on crown segmentation quality, which degrades when canopies close and crowns overlap. Additionally, our training plots are few and drawn from public land, so private woodlands may differ. Section 6 Discussion. Our results suggest that drone-based structural learning is a viable alternative to harvest-plot calibration for biomass inventories, with applications extending to any region where drones can be flown.
